notes:
The first rupee of the Republic. Struck in only two years — 1950 and 1954 — before decimalisation swept away annas and pies in 1957, making this the last rupee of the old sixteen-anna system.

The obverse carries the Lion Capital of Ashoka above the legend GOVERNMENT OF INDIA, the emblem adopted in 1950 to replace the profile of George VI. The reverse gives the denomination in Hindi and English, flanked by ears of wheat — a deliberate nod to the agricultural priorities of the first Five-Year Plan.

The star beneath the Lion Capital is the mark of the Hyderabad mint.

The smallest coin of the 1988 stainless-steel series, and the last ten paise India struck — the denomination was discontinued in 1998 and demonetised in 2011.

Stainless steel replaced aluminium across the minor denominations that year: cheaper to strike, far more durable, and no longer worth more as scrap than as money.

The reverse carries an Indian one-horned rhinoceros — part of a run of wildlife designs that broke from the emblems and portraits of earlier coinage.

The rhino was a conservation emblem: hunted to a few hundred animals by the early twentieth century, it had recovered in Kaziranga and Assam by the time this coin was struck.

The reverse shows Sansad Bhavan, the circular Parliament House in New Delhi, set against an outline map of India.

Completed in 1927 to a Lutyens and Baker design, its colonnaded drum was chosen here as shorthand for the Republic itself.

Two ears of grain flank the denomination — the same agricultural motif carried by the very first rupee of the Republic in 1950, redrawn for a stainless-steel coin more than forty years later.

Stainless steel arrived for the rupee in 1992, replacing copper-nickel.

The National Integration type: a map of India overlaid with four hands, struck on an eleven-sided flan.

The hendecagonal shape was deliberate — it let people tell two rupees from one by touch alone, a considerable practical advantage in a country with many languages and scripts.

Heavy for its size at nine grams — noticeably weightier than the stainless-steel rupee beside it, and the densest coin in ordinary circulation at the time.

The denomination is flanked by stylised floral sprays. The edge is reeded with a groove.
